headline: 🔥 TENEMENT FIRE — 12 DEAD, BLAME UNCLEAR
factoid: New York City had over 80,000 tenement buildings by 1900, with frequent deadly fires. The penny press routinely raced to assign blame — to immigrants, to slumlords, to political ward bosses — before fire marshals could investigate. Joseph Pulitzer's New York World built much of its early circulation on these stories.

headline: 🔥 MAYOR SEEN LEAVING ACTRESS'S BROWNSTONE
factoid: Public figures' private lives were standard penny-press fodder from the 1830s onward. James Gordon Bennett's New York Herald pioneered the practice; by the 1890s every major U.S. city had multiple competing dailies running political-figure scandal as front-page news.

headline: 🔥 RIVAL PAPER MISSPELLS PRESIDENT'S NAME
factoid: Hearst's New York Journal and Pulitzer's New York World ran a years-long public feud (1895-1898), each headline a chance to mock the other's errors. The phrase 'yellow journalism' originated from a comic strip ('The Yellow Kid') that both papers ran in competing versions.

headline: 🔥 STEAMER LOST OFF MONTAUK — NAMES INSIDE
factoid: The USS Maine explosion in Havana Harbor (Feb 1898) was attributed by Hearst's Journal to Spanish sabotage within hours. A 1976 U.S. Navy investigation concluded the explosion was most likely caused by an internal coal-bunker fire. The Spanish-American War followed regardless.

headline: 🔥 EXTRA! WAR DECLARED — DETAILS TO FOLLOW
factoid: Hearst's directive to illustrator Frederic Remington in Havana (1897) — 'You furnish the pictures and I'll furnish the war' — is contested as apocryphal, but it accurately describes the editorial posture of the New York Journal's pre-war coverage.

headline: ⚡ FRENZY: STOP-PRESS RUSH — NEWSBOYS SHOUTING ON EVERY CORNER
factoid: By 1900 major U.S. newspapers were issuing 5-7 'Extra' editions per day during breaking news cycles. The phrase 'Extra! Extra! Read all about it!' described a real operational rhythm — newsboys would shout-sell each new edition on Manhattan street corners within 30 minutes of presses starting.
